found-vitals-l01.q: You count 19 beats in 15 seconds on a patient with a regular pulse. What is the rate, and what is the built-in weakness of this method?
choices: 76, and a one-beat miscount shifts the reported rate by 4
76, and the method has no error at all
19, since the count is already per minute
38, because you double a 15-second count
found-vitals-l01.why: A 15-second count is multiplied by 4, so 19 x 4 = 76, and that same multiplier magnifies any single-beat error into 4 beats per minute. Doubling is for a 30-second count, and the raw count is never the rate.

found-vitals-l01.q: An adult in a car crash has a strong carotid pulse but you cannot feel a radial pulse on either wrist. What does that tell you first?
choices: Both wrists are probably fractured
Peripheral perfusion is failing, which is a shock finding
The systolic pressure is exactly 80 mmHg
Nothing, since radial pulses are often absent in healthy adults
found-vitals-l01.why: Pulses are lost from the outside in as perfusion falls, so a central pulse without a peripheral one means peripheral flow has already dropped. The old teaching that assigns an exact systolic to each site is not reliable enough to quote as a number, and bilateral wrist fractures would be a coincidence, not an explanation.

found-vitals-l02.q: A 30-year-old with a rib injury breathes 22 times a minute with barely visible chest rise. A second patient breathes 24 times a minute with full, easy chest rise. Which patient worries you more?
choices: The second patient, because the rate is higher
Neither, both rates are near normal
The first patient, because shallow breaths move less air despite a similar rate
Impossible to say without a pulse oximeter
found-vitals-l02.why: The air actually reaching gas exchange is rate multiplied by depth, so a shallow 22 moves far less than a full 24. Rate alone is the weakest of the four axes, and an SpO2 can still read normal early in a patient who is under-ventilating.

found-vitals-l02.q: You hear coarse gurgling from an unresponsive patient's mouth on every breath. What is your first action?
choices: Apply a non-rebreather at 15 L
Listen to the lungs with a stethoscope
Start a bronchodilator treatment
Suction the airway
found-vitals-l02.why: Gurgling means fluid sitting in the upper airway, and oxygen delivered on top of fluid just pushes it further in. Suction first, then oxygenate; a stethoscope and a bronchodilator address lower-airway problems this patient does not yet have.

found-vitals-l03.q: You palpate the radial pulse and it disappears at 130 mmHg. To what pressure should you inflate for the auscultated reading?
choices: 150 to 160 mmHg
130 mmHg exactly
180 to 200 mmHg
110 to 120 mmHg
found-vitals-l03.why: The rule is 20 to 30 mmHg above the palpated estimate, so 150 to 160. Stopping at the estimate puts you at or below the true systolic, and grossly over-inflating is painful and can cause venous congestion that distorts the diastolic.

found-vitals-l03.q: The only available arm has a running intravenous line, and the other arm has a dialysis fistula. What is the correct move?
choices: Take the pressure over the intravenous line anyway
Use the fistula arm, since a fistula does not affect the reading
Use an appropriately sized cuff on the thigh or forearm and document the site
Skip the blood pressure entirely and chart it as refused
found-vitals-l03.why: Both listed arms are excluded, so an alternative site with a correctly sized cuff and a documented location is the answer. Cuffing a fistula can damage it, cuffing over a running line ruins both the line and the number, and omitting a pressure without an attempt or a reason leaves the chart unreadable.

found-vitals-l04.q: A patient reads 150/60. What is the pulse pressure and what is the MAP?
choices: Pulse pressure 60, MAP 105
Pulse pressure 90, MAP 90
Pulse pressure 90, MAP 105
Pulse pressure 60, MAP 90
found-vitals-l04.why: Pulse pressure is 150 minus 60 = 90, which is wide. MAP is (150 + 120) / 3 = 90 mmHg. Using the systolic average instead of the diastolic-weighted formula is the usual error and overestimates the mean.

found-vitals-l04.q: An automatic cuff on a cool, mottled patient reports 104/62 while the patient looks poorly perfused. What should you do with that number?
choices: Accept it, since the machine is more objective than a person
Repeat it on the same arm with the same machine until it agrees
Chart it and re-check in 15 minutes
Confirm it manually, because oscillometric devices tend to over-read genuinely low pressures
found-vitals-l04.why: Oscillometric machines calculate from oscillation amplitude, and at low pressures the signal compresses so the device reads higher than the truth, which is the most dangerous direction of error. Repeating on the same machine reproduces the same bias, and waiting 15 minutes on a poorly perfused patient wastes the time you have.

found-vitals-l05.q: A patient with hemoglobin of 5 g/dL after a slow gastrointestinal bleed reads SpO2 99% on room air. What is wrong with treating that as reassurance?
choices: Nothing, 99% means oxygen delivery is adequate
Saturation is the percentage of hemoglobin that is loaded, and there is very little hemoglobin to load
The probe overestimates in anemia by exactly 10%
The reading proves the bleed has stopped
found-vitals-l05.why: The device reports the fraction of hemoglobin seats that are filled, not how many seats exist, so a severely anemic patient can be fully saturated and still oxygen-starved. There is no fixed percentage correction, and saturation says nothing about ongoing blood loss.

found-vitals-l05.q: A patient with acrylic nails and dark polish gives an erratic SpO2 in the low 80s while looking comfortable and speaking full sentences. What is the best next step?
choices: Intubate for a saturation under 85%
Chart the value and move on
Remove the polish or turn the probe sideways across the finger, or move to an earlobe
Increase oxygen to 15 L by non-rebreather and re-check in an hour
found-vitals-l05.why: Dark polish and artificial nails block the light path and produce falsely low or erratic readings, and the fix is to clear the path or change the site. Treating an artifact as a true saturation escalates care the patient does not need, and charting an unreliable number without a note misleads the next reader.

found-vitals-l06.q: A patient has a temperature of 101.8 F. What is that in Celsius, and is it a fever?
choices: 38.8 C, yes
39.6 C, yes
38.0 C, exactly at the threshold
found-vitals-l06.why: (101.8 - 32) x 5/9 = 38.8 C, which is above the 38.0 C (100.4 F) fever threshold. Converting in the wrong direction or subtracting after the multiplication produces the other values here.

found-vitals-l06.q: A patient with a kidney stone rates the pain 9 out of 10, and after medication rates it 5. Which part of that is the clinically useful information?
choices: Only the 9, since it shows the pain was real
The 4-point change, because response to treatment is what the number is for
Only the 5, since it is the current state
Neither, because a self-reported number cannot be trusted
found-vitals-l06.why: Pain scores are subjective, so their value is in the trend and the treatment response rather than in the absolute figure. Self-report remains the reference standard for pain, so dismissing the number outright is wrong.

found-vitals-l07.q: A head-injured patient does not open his eyes at all, makes incomprehensible groaning sounds, and his arms bend inward across his chest when you apply pressure. What is his GCS?
choices: GCS 7 (E1 V3 M3)
GCS 5 (E1 V2 M2)
GCS 6 (E1 V2 M3)
GCS 8 (E2 V2 M4)
found-vitals-l07.why: No eye opening is E1, incomprehensible sounds are V2, and abnormal flexion with the arms bending inward is decorticate posturing at M3, totaling 6. Extension outward would be M2 and withdrawal away from the stimulus would be M4.

found-vitals-l07.q: A patient is found unconscious and smelling of alcohol. Which action comes first?
choices: Let him sleep it off and re-check in an hour
Check a blood glucose
Document intoxication and restrain him
Obtain an orthostatic blood pressure
found-vitals-l07.why: Hypoglycemia imitates intoxication exactly and reverses within minutes, so a fingerstick is the reversible cause you rule out first. Assuming alcohol and waiting lets a treatable brain continue to starve, and orthostatics are meaningless in an unconscious patient.

found-vitals-l08.q: What is the expected systolic pressure for a 6-year-old, and what is the floor?
choices: Expected 82, floor 62
Expected 96, floor 76
Expected 102, floor 82
Expected 100, floor 80
found-vitals-l08.why: Expected is 90 + (2 x 6) = 102 and the floor is 70 + (2 x 6) = 82. The gap between those two numbers is the child's whole reserve, and swapping the constants or the multiplier produces the other options.

found-vitals-l08.q: An 82-year-old on metoprolol is bleeding internally. Why might her heart rate stay near 70?
choices: Beta blockade plus age-related blunting prevents the compensatory tachycardia
Older adults do not lose blood as quickly
Metoprolol increases blood volume
A heart rate near 70 proves the bleeding is minor
found-vitals-l08.why: Beta blockers block the sympathetic signal that would normally raise the rate, and the aging heart responds less to that signal anyway, so the usual early warning simply does not appear. The drug does nothing to blood volume, and a normal-looking pulse in this patient is the opposite of reassuring.

found-vitals-l09.q: A patient reads HR 96 and BP 112/68. What is the shock index and how is it read?
choices: 1.17, treat as shock
0.86, borderline, look harder
0.61, normal
1.41, emergency
found-vitals-l09.why: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure, so 96 / 112 = 0.86, which lands in the 0.7 to 0.9 borderline band. Dividing systolic by heart rate or using the diastolic produces the other values here.

found-vitals-l09.q: You give a dose of medication that affects blood pressure. When should vitals be taken?
choices: Only once afterward, at the end of the shift
Only before, so you have a baseline on file
Before the dose and again after it
Whenever the patient asks
found-vitals-l09.why: A post-dose number without a pre-dose number cannot show whether the drug worked or harmed, and a pre-dose number alone shows nothing about the effect. Pairing them is what makes the intervention interpretable.

found-vitals-l10.q: A 7-month-old has a respiratory rate of 68 that has been sustained for twenty minutes. How do you read that?
choices: Normal, since infants breathe 25 to 50 and short bursts are expected
Normal only if the infant is crying
Abnormal at any infant age band and needs explanation
Impossible, since infants cannot sustain that rate
found-vitals-l10.why: A sustained rate over 60 in an infant is abnormal in every age band, and 68 is well past that line. Crying can briefly raise a rate, but it does not make a sustained 68 normal.

found-vitals-l10.q: A newborn has repeated breathing pauses of about 8 seconds with no color change and no heart rate drop. What is this and what do you do?
choices: Apnea; begin bag-mask ventilation
Periodic breathing, which is normal in a newborn; continue monitoring
Agonal breathing; begin compressions
Cheyne-Stokes breathing; suspect a head injury
found-vitals-l10.why: Pauses under 20 seconds with no cyanosis and no bradycardia are periodic breathing, a normal newborn pattern. A pause of 20 seconds or more, or any pause with a color or rate change, is apnea and would require intervention.

found-vitals-l11.q: A patient with a respiratory rate of 16 has an EtCO2 of 62 mmHg and a plateau that is present but tall. What does this combination mean?
choices: Normal ventilation, since the rate is 12 to 20
Hyperventilation, because the plateau is intact
Equipment failure, since a rate of 16 cannot produce that number
The rate is normal but carbon dioxide is not being cleared, so ventilation is inadequate
found-vitals-l11.why: A rate counts events and says nothing about the air moved, so a normal-looking 16 with an EtCO2 of 62 means retained carbon dioxide from shallow or obstructed breaths. Hyperventilation drives EtCO2 below 35, in the opposite direction.

found-vitals-l11.q: Immediately after an intubation attempt the capnogram is a flat line at zero with compressions in progress. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: The tube is not in the trachea, or there is no circulation delivering carbon dioxide
The patient is hyperventilating
The waveform is normal for a tubed patient
The sensor needs 5 minutes to warm up
found-vitals-l11.why: No exhaled carbon dioxide at all points to an esophageal tube, a disconnection, or no blood reaching the lungs. A correctly placed tube with ongoing compressions should show a waveform, usually with an EtCO2 above 10 mmHg.

found-vitals-l12.q: You take a pressure, get a surprising result, and immediately re-inflate the same arm. What error does that introduce?
choices: None, immediate repeats are preferred
Venous congestion raises the diastolic reading
The systolic is lost entirely
The cuff loses calibration
found-vitals-l12.why: Blood pooled from the first inflation has not drained, and that congestion pushes the diastolic up. Waiting 1 to 2 minutes, or alternating arms, prevents it; cuff calibration is unaffected by how soon you repeat.

found-vitals-l12.q: Your first assessment of a new patient gives 152/88 in the right arm. What should you do about the left arm?
choices: Nothing, one arm is sufficient at a first assessment
Measure it only if the patient reports arm pain
Measure it too, and investigate a consistent difference over 10 to 15 mmHg
Measure it and average the two values
found-vitals-l12.why: Both arms are measured at a first assessment because a consistent systolic difference over 10 to 15 mmHg can indicate subclavian stenosis or, in the right setting, aortic dissection. Averaging hides the finding, and the higher arm is the one used from then on.

found-vitals-l13.q: A patient who speaks only Haitian Creole is in pain and her adult son offers to translate. What is the correct approach?
choices: Use the son, since he knows her best
Use a trained interpreter, because family members summarize and soften
Use gestures and skip the pain score
Score her with FLACC instead
found-vitals-l13.why: Family translators condense, soften and sometimes answer on the patient's behalf, so a trained interpreter is required for an accurate self-report. Self-report is still available here, which means an observational tool like FLACC is not the right substitute.

found-vitals-l13.q: A nursing home patient with dementia scores PAINAD 8. After acetaminophen she scores PAINAD 3. What does that document?
choices: That she was never in real pain
That she is now sedated
That the observed behaviors improved after treatment, which supports pain as the cause
Nothing, because PAINAD cannot be repeated
found-vitals-l13.why: PAINAD is scored 0 to 10 precisely so it can be trended, and a drop after an analgesic trial is evidence the behavior was driven by pain. Acetaminophen is not a sedative, and a falling score is the intended use of the tool, not a misuse.

found-vitals-l14.q: Which route and threshold are required to apply the infant fever rule in a 5-week-old?
choices: Axillary, 37.5 C
Temporal, 38.5 C
Tympanic, 38.0 C
Rectal, 38.0 C (100.4 F)
found-vitals-l14.why: The rule is written for a rectal temperature of 38.0 C (100.4 F) or higher, and only that route supports the decision. Axillary, temporal and tympanic readings are screens whose offsets are too variable to trigger an emergency infant evaluation.
(39.4 x 9/5) + 32 = 70.9 + 32 = 102.9 F. Remembering that 40 C is 104 F makes 39.4 C land just under it, which rules out the higher and much lower options at a glance.

found-vitals-l15.q: A head-injured patient goes HR 92 to 74 to 56, BP 138/82 to 168/84 to 196/80, with breathing that has become irregular. What pattern is this?
choices: Hypovolemic shock
Cushing's triad from rising intracranial pressure
An expected response to pain medication
Improving perfusion after fluid
found-vitals-l15.why: Rising systolic with widening pulse pressure, falling heart rate and irregular respirations is Cushing's triad, a late sign of rising pressure inside the skull. Hypovolemic shock moves the opposite way, with a rising rate and a falling pressure.

found-vitals-l15.q: A dehydrated toddler goes from HR 168 to 132 with capillary refill improving from 4 seconds to 2 and is now alert and drinking. Why is this falling heart rate real improvement, unlike a falling rate in a shocked child?
choices: Because any heart rate moving toward normal is improvement
Because toddlers do not develop bradycardia
Because the perfusion and appearance findings moved in the same good direction
Because capillary refill is the only finding that matters
found-vitals-l15.why: A number only means something inside the story, and here refill and interactiveness improved alongside the rate, which confirms recovery. In the dangerous version the rate falls while the child goes limp and mottled, which is the descent toward arrest.

found-vitals-l16.q: A patient at 28 weeks gestation becomes lightheaded and pale within a minute of being laid flat on a backboard. What is the first action?
choices: Give a fluid bolus and re-check in 10 minutes
Sit her fully upright
Roll her left or apply manual left uterine displacement
Apply oxygen and continue flat positioning
found-vitals-l16.why: After about 20 weeks the uterus compresses the inferior vena cava when the patient lies flat, cutting venous return, and left lateral tilt or manual left uterine displacement relieves it within seconds. Fluids and oxygen do not address the mechanical obstruction, and sitting fully upright is unnecessary and often unsafe on a board.

found-vitals-l16.q: A runner collapses roughly 30 seconds after crossing a finish line and is alert with a normal temperature. A second runner collapses mid-race while still running. Which one worries you more, and why?
choices: The first, because post-race collapse is always cardiac
The second, because collapse during exertion is cardiac until proven otherwise
Neither, both are benign exercise-associated collapse
Both equally, since collapse timing carries no information
found-vitals-l16.why: Collapse after the finish line is usually benign exercise-associated collapse from blood pooling once the leg muscle pump stops. Collapse during exertion is the pattern associated with cardiac causes and is treated as such until ruled out.

found-vitals-l17.q: A patient's saturation is 95% on 6 L by nasal cannula. Why does NEWS2 still assign points?
choices: Because nasal cannula readings are inaccurate
Because oxygen use always indicates an infection
Because the score penalizes any device attached to a patient
Because achieving 95% only with support is a sicker patient than 95% on room air
found-vitals-l17.why: The score awards points for supplemental oxygen independently so that a saturation propped up by support cannot look identical to an unsupported one. It has nothing to do with device accuracy or the cause of the oxygen requirement.

found-vitals-l17.q: You hand off a patient. Which statement carries the most information?
choices: Her heart rate is 122.
Her vitals are a bit off.
Her rate has gone 88, 104 then 122 over the last forty minutes, with her pressure falling from 128/72 to 104/58.
She looks unwell but the numbers are fine.
found-vitals-l17.why: Timed sets with a stated direction let the next clinician see the trajectory, which is what decisions are made on. A single value gives position without direction, and vague impressions give neither.

quiz.q: You count 21 beats in 15 seconds on a patient with a regular rhythm. What rate do you report?
quiz.why: A 15-second count is multiplied by 4, so 21 x 4 = 84. Doubling gives the 30-second answer, reporting the raw count ignores the interval, and multiplying by 6 is the conversion for a 10-second count.

quiz.q: While checking an unresponsive adult's carotid pulse, a partner reaches for the opposite carotid to compare. What should you tell them?
choices: Check one side only, because compressing both reduces blood flow to the brain
Compare both sides, since a difference is diagnostic of stroke
Use both sides but press only lightly
Compare both sides but only for 5 seconds
quiz.why: Compressing both carotids at once can cut cerebral perfusion, so only one side is checked at a time regardless of pressure or duration. Heavy pressure also risks a vagal response that slows the heart, which is a second reason to be gentle.

quiz.q: A 68-year-old with atrial fibrillation has a pulse you cannot find a pattern in. Your partner counts 15 seconds and reports 96. What is the problem?
choices: Nothing, 15-second counts are accurate in any rhythm
The multiplier should have been 2 rather than 4
The radial site is invalid in atrial fibrillation
A short count assumes evenly spaced beats, which an irregular rhythm breaks
quiz.why: Sampling 15 seconds and multiplying assumes the beats are spread evenly across the minute, and an irregular rhythm violates that, so the number can be far off. The radial site is fine; it is the interval that must be a full 60 seconds.

quiz.q: A 3-year-old with a barking cough has a high-pitched noise you can hear across the room when she breathes in. What does this describe and where does it come from?
choices: Wheezing, from narrowed lower airways
Stridor, from narrowing at or above the larynx
Crackles, from fluid in the alveoli
Grunting, from exhaling against a closed throat
quiz.why: A high-pitched noise on inhalation is stridor, which comes from upper airway narrowing such as croup, swelling, or a foreign body. Wheezing is heard mostly on exhalation from lower airways, crackles are fine popping on inhalation, and grunting occurs on exhalation.

quiz.q: A patient with new diabetes is breathing deeply, rapidly and with a sighing quality, and his breath smells faintly fruity. What pattern is this and why is it happening?
choices: Cheyne-Stokes breathing, from a brain injury
Kussmaul respirations, blowing off carbon dioxide to offset metabolic acid
Agonal breathing, from early cardiac arrest
Periodic breathing, a normal variant
quiz.why: Deep, fast, sighing breaths in diabetic ketoacidosis are Kussmaul respirations, the body clearing carbon dioxide to compensate for acid buildup. Cheyne-Stokes cycles deeper and shallower with pauses, agonal breathing is slow gasping in arrest, and periodic breathing is a newborn finding.

quiz.q: A patient with heart failure can say only two or three words before pausing for a breath. How should you record this?
choices: Respirations normal, patient talking
Anxiety-related shortness of breath
Mild dyspnea
Speaking in two-to-three-word phrases, which is a severity finding to re-check later
quiz.why: How many words a patient can say in one breath is a free, repeatable severity scale, and writing it down creates a trend anyone can interpret. Calling it mild or anxiety-related substitutes an impression for an observation, and the patient is clearly not breathing normally.

quiz.q: You palpate the radial pulse, and it vanishes as the cuff reaches 150 mmHg. To what pressure should you inflate for the auscultated reading?
choices: 170 to 180 mmHg
150 mmHg
200 mmHg
130 mmHg
quiz.why: Standard practice is 20 to 30 mmHg above the palpated estimate, so 170 to 180. Inflating only to the estimate starts you at or below the true systolic, and inflating far higher is painful and causes venous congestion that distorts the diastolic.

quiz.q: Why do Korotkoff sounds exist only between full occlusion and no cuff pressure?
choices: The cuff bladder vibrates at intermediate pressures
The stethoscope only transmits sound in that range
Sound requires turbulent flow, which occurs only when the artery is partly narrowed
The artery spasms when partly compressed
quiz.why: A fully open artery has smooth, silent flow and a fully closed one has no flow at all, so audible turbulence exists only in the partly narrowed middle. That is precisely why the beginning and end of the sound define the systolic and diastolic values.

quiz.q: A very thin, frail 91-year-old is measured with a standard adult cuff and reads 88/50. What error should you consider first?
choices: Too-small cuff, reading falsely low
Too-small cuff, reading falsely high
Too-large cuff, reading falsely high
Too-large cuff, reading falsely low
quiz.why: On a thin arm a standard cuff is effectively oversized, and an oversized bladder compresses the artery with less pressure, so the gauge understates the truth. That direction of error can invent a hypotension that is not there; an undersized cuff produces the opposite mistake.

quiz.q: In the back of a moving ambulance the siren makes auscultation impossible on a critical patient. What is the appropriate action?
choices: Estimate the pressure from the strength of the radial pulse
Obtain a palpated systolic and chart it as a number over P
Skip the blood pressure until arrival
Chart the last reading from the scene as current
quiz.why: Palpation gives a real systolic, charted as for example 92/P, which tells the next reader both the value and the method. Guessing from pulse strength is not reliable, omitting the pressure on a critical patient loses the trend, and copying a prior set forward is falsification.

quiz.q: A septic patient reads 96/44. What is the MAP, and how does it compare with the usual resuscitation target?
choices: 70 mmHg, comfortably above target
61 mmHg, above target
61 mmHg, below the 65 mmHg target
70 mmHg, below target
quiz.why: MAP is (96 + 88) / 3 = 184 / 3 = 61 mmHg, which sits under the 65 mmHg floor used as the standard target in shock and sepsis care. The systolic of 96 looks tolerable, which is exactly the trap the formula exists to catch.

quiz.q: A patient with a stab wound to the chest becomes progressively worse with a blood pressure moving from 118/74 to 96/78. What does the narrowing pulse pressure suggest?
choices: Falling stroke volume with clamped vessels, as in tamponade or hypovolemia
Vasodilation from a spinal injury
Rising pressure inside the skull
A measurement error from a too-large cuff
quiz.why: Pulse pressure falls from 44 to 18 as the diastolic climbs toward the systolic, which is arteriolar clamping around a shrinking stroke volume, classic for tamponade or blood loss. Vasodilation and rising intracranial pressure widen rather than narrow the pulse pressure.

quiz.q: A patient with three days of diarrhea has supine vitals of HR 84 and BP 122/74. At one minute standing he is HR 98 and BP 116/70 but becomes gray and nearly faints. How do you score the test?
choices: Positive, because symptoms on standing count regardless of the numbers
Negative, because no threshold was crossed
Invalid, because the test must be repeated at 3 minutes
Negative, because the heart rate rose less than 20
quiz.why: Near-syncope on standing is itself a positive result and outranks the numeric criteria, which are the 20 mmHg systolic drop, 10 mmHg diastolic drop and 20 bpm rate rise. Waiting for a 3-minute repeat on a patient who is about to faint adds nothing but risk.

quiz.q: A patient in rapid atrial fibrillation has an automatic cuff that re-inflates three times before displaying 118/62. How should the number be treated?
choices: Accurate, because the machine repeated until confident
Accurate for the systolic only
Unreliable, because irregular rhythms confuse oscillometric analysis
Unreliable only if the patient was moving
quiz.why: Oscillometric devices identify the peak oscillation and calculate from it, and beat-to-beat variability in atrial fibrillation corrupts that analysis. Repeated re-inflation signals failed attempts rather than added confidence, so a manual reading is needed before acting.

quiz.q: A patient with a hemoglobin of 4.8 g/dL after a long gastrointestinal bleed reads SpO2 100% on room air. What is the correct interpretation?
choices: Oxygen delivery is adequate and no oxygen is needed
Saturation is normal but the oxygen-carrying capacity is severely reduced
The oximeter is broken and should be replaced
The reading proves carbon monoxide poisoning
quiz.why: Pulse oximetry reports the percentage of hemoglobin that is loaded, not how much hemoglobin exists, so nearly empty blood can be fully saturated. Carbon monoxide also produces a falsely high reading, but nothing in this history points to it.

quiz.q: A COPD patient at his chronic baseline reads SpO2 90%. What is the usual target range for this population?
choices: Above 96%
Above 94% like any other adult
88% to 92% in many protocols
quiz.why: Many chronic COPD protocols target 88% to 92% rather than the general adult threshold of 94%, so 90% sits inside the intended range. Driving these patients to the high 90s is not the goal, and protocols vary, so the local one governs.

quiz.q: A patient is tripoding, speaking one word at a time, and visibly straining, with an SpO2 of 97% on room air. What is the correct response?
choices: Reassure the patient, since the saturation is normal
Repeat the saturation on the other hand and then reassess
Treat the breathing emergency the patient is showing you, regardless of the number
Withhold oxygen until the saturation falls below 94%
quiz.why: Saturation is a late-moving number and a patient can be in severe respiratory failure with a normal SpO2 for some time. The clinical picture outranks the display, and delaying care until the number catches up wastes the compensated window.

quiz.q: A patient's temperature is 35.6 C. How is that classified?
choices: Normal
Fever
Severe hypothermia
Below the normal range but above the 35.0 C hypothermia threshold
quiz.why: Hypothermia begins below 35.0 C, so 35.6 C is low but not yet hypothermic, and normal runs about 36.5 to 37.5 C. Severe hypothermia is below 28 C, and fever begins at 38.0 C in the opposite direction.

quiz.q: A patient with influenza has a temperature of 39.2 C and is shivering under blankets saying she feels freezing. Why does she feel cold while running hot?
choices: Her skin temperature is genuinely low while her core is high
Her hypothalamic set point has been raised, so her actual temperature feels too cold to her body
Shivering always means hypothermia
The thermometer is reading the wrong route
quiz.why: In fever the thermostat itself is reset upward, so the body treats its current temperature as too low and shivers to reach the new set point. That raised set point is also why antipyretics work in fever and do nothing in environmental hyperthermia.

quiz.q: A patient describes chest discomfort that worsens when you press on the sternum. What can you conclude?
choices: It is definitely musculoskeletal and cardiac causes are excluded
It is definitely cardiac, since palpation should not change chest pain
Reproducible chest wall pain leans musculoskeletal but never rules out a heart attack
Palpation findings carry no information at all
quiz.why: Pain reproduced by chest wall pressure makes a musculoskeletal cause more likely, but that finding alone has never been reliable enough to exclude an acute coronary event. The PQRST elements shift probability rather than deliver a diagnosis.

quiz.q: A patient does not open her eyes, makes no sound at all, and her arms straighten and rotate outward when pressure is applied. What is her GCS?
choices: GCS 3 (E1 V1 M1)
GCS 4 (E1 V1 M2)
GCS 5 (E1 V1 M3)
GCS 6 (E2 V1 M3)
quiz.why: No eye opening is E1, no verbal response is V1, and extension with outward rotation is decerebrate posturing scored M2, totaling 4. Abnormal inward flexion would be M3, and a total of 3 requires no motor response at all.

quiz.q: A patient knows his own name but cannot say where he is, what month it is, or what happened. How is his orientation documented?
choices: Alert and oriented x1
Alert and oriented x4
Responsive to verbal stimulus only
Unresponsive
quiz.why: Orientation is graded to person, place, time and event, and this patient retains only person, so he is A and O x1. He is alert because his eyes are open and he is interacting, which rules out the verbal and unresponsive levels of AVPU.

quiz.q: A patient with a fingerstick glucose of 46 mg/dL is confused, sweating and combative. How is this best described?
choices: Normal glucose with a psychiatric cause
Mild hyperglycemia
Diabetic ketoacidosis
Clinically significant hypoglycemia, which reverses within minutes of treatment
quiz.why: A glucose under 54 mg/dL is clinically significant hypoglycemia, and confusion, sweating and combativeness are its classic presentation. Diabetic ketoacidosis runs high, often over 250 mg/dL, and attributing this to psychiatric causes delays a treatment that works in minutes.

quiz.q: A colleague wipes the finger with alcohol and lances it immediately, then squeezes the fingertip hard to produce a drop. What is the expected effect on the result?
choices: The reading will be falsely high from tissue fluid
No effect, since the meter corrects for dilution
The reading may be falsely low from alcohol and interstitial fluid diluting the sample
The meter will refuse to read the sample
quiz.why: Wet alcohol and milked interstitial fluid both dilute the blood, which shifts the value downward. Letting the alcohol dry, wiping away the first drop, and testing the second without hard squeezing avoids it; meters do not correct for contamination.

quiz.q: What is the expected systolic blood pressure for a 4-year-old?
choices: 78 mmHg
84 mmHg
90 mmHg
98 mmHg
quiz.why: The expected value for ages 1 to 10 is 90 + (2 x age), so 90 + 8 = 98 mmHg. The minimum acceptable systolic uses 70 as the constant, giving 78, which is the floor rather than the expected value.

quiz.q: A 9-year-old struck by a bicycle has a systolic of 92, a heart rate of 148 and capillary refill of 4 seconds. How should this be read?
choices: Normal, because the pressure is above the floor of 88
Abnormal only because of the heart rate
Compensated shock, because the pressure holds while rate and perfusion are abnormal
Decompensated shock, because the pressure is below the floor
quiz.why: The floor is 70 + (2 x 9) = 88 mmHg, so a systolic of 92 is still above it, but a rate of 148 and refill of 4 seconds show hard compensation. A normal pediatric pressure is never reassurance on its own; hypotension would mean the reserve is already gone.

quiz.q: An 80-year-old with a long history of untreated hypertension arrives with a systolic of 112 and new confusion. Why should this concern you?
choices: A systolic of 112 may be a substantial drop from this person's own baseline
112 is below the adult hypotension threshold of 120
Confusion is a normal finding at age 80
Older adults should always run above 160 systolic
quiz.why: Vitals are judged against the individual's baseline, and a chronically hypertensive patient can be significantly hypotensive at a number that looks normal on a population range. The adult hypotension marker is a systolic under 90, and new confusion is never a normal aging finding.

quiz.q: How often should vital signs be repeated on a patient you have judged unstable?
choices: Every 30 minutes
Every 5 minutes
Every 15 minutes
Once per hour
quiz.why: Unstable patients and patients who have just received a significant intervention are reassessed every 5 minutes, which is often enough to catch a change while you can still act on it. Every 15 minutes is the stable-patient interval, and longer intervals lose the trend.

quiz.q: A patient reads HR 132 and BP 88/54. What is the shock index and what does it mean?
choices: 1.5, well over 1.0, so treat as shock
0.67, normal
0.85, borderline
2.4, meaningless because the value exceeds the scale
quiz.why: Shock index is heart rate divided by systolic pressure, so 132 / 88 = 1.5, meaning the rate has far exceeded the systolic. Values over 0.9 already carry increased mortality and transfusion risk, and there is no upper cutoff that makes the index invalid.

quiz.q: A patient is too combative for a blood pressure to be obtained. What should the chart show?
choices: A blank field
Unable to obtain BP, patient combative, with the time
An estimate based on the pulse quality
The previous reading carried forward
quiz.why: A stated reason is clinical information in itself and tells the next reader that an attempt was made and why it failed. A blank is unreadable, an estimate is invented data, and copying a previous set forward falsifies the record.

quiz.q: Which three observations make up the Pediatric Assessment Triangle?
choices: Heart rate, respiratory rate, blood pressure
Airway, breathing, circulation
Appearance, work of breathing, circulation to skin
Temperature, capillary refill, mental status
quiz.why: The triangle is appearance, work of breathing and circulation to skin, all assessed from across the room before touching the child. It is deliberately not a set of measured numbers, which is what makes it faster and more sensitive than a vitals set.

quiz.q: An 8-month-old with sepsis has a heart rate of 54 and mottled, cool skin. What does current practice call for?
choices: Observation, since the rate is within an acceptable range for sleep
Fluids only, since the rate will rise with volume
Warm the infant and re-check in 10 minutes
Chest compressions, because a rate under 60 with poor perfusion in an infant is a compression indication
quiz.why: A heart rate under 60 with signs of poor perfusion in an infant or child means compressions, because a slowing pediatric heart has run out of oxygen. Waiting, warming or relying on fluids alone all spend the minutes that decide the outcome.

quiz.q: A prehospital protocol does not require a blood pressure in children under 3. What is the reasoning?
choices: Children under 3 do not have measurable blood pressure
Cuffs small enough do not exist
It is slow and unreliable, and the decision has already been made by rate, effort, skin and appearance
Blood pressure in small children is always normal
quiz.why: In small children a pressure is difficult to obtain, frequently inaccurate, and arrives after the findings that actually decide care. Cuffs do exist and pressures are measurable; the point is that the measurement rarely changes the plan in that age group.

quiz.q: What is the normal range for end-tidal carbon dioxide, and what question does it answer?
choices: 35 to 45 mmHg, and it answers whether air is actually moving
35 to 45 mmHg, and it answers whether hemoglobin is loaded
90 to 100 mmHg, and it answers whether the patient is perfusing
12 to 20 mmHg, and it answers the respiratory rate
quiz.why: EtCO2 runs 35 to 45 mmHg and reflects ventilation, meaning whether air is moving in and out. Whether hemoglobin is loaded is the question SpO2 answers, which is why both monitors exist and fail at different moments.

quiz.q: During a resuscitation the EtCO2 has been 16 mmHg and suddenly climbs to 39 mmHg with no change in compression technique. What does this most likely mean?
choices: The capnography sensor has failed
Return of spontaneous circulation
The tube has moved into the esophagus
Compressions have become too shallow
quiz.why: A sudden rise into the normal range means far more blood is reaching the lungs, which usually signals return of circulation and often appears before a pulse can be felt. An esophageal tube or failing compressions would drive the value down, not up.

quiz.q: A shocked patient's monitor shows SpO2 88% with a damped, irregular pleth waveform. How should you act?
choices: Accept 88% and titrate oxygen to that value
Ignore oxygen entirely until a waveform appears
Assume the true saturation is exactly 98%
Treat the number as unreliable, improve the signal or change the site, and manage the patient clinically
quiz.why: A poor waveform means the device is not tracking a clean arterial pulse, so the number above it cannot be trusted in either direction. The right response is to fix the signal, by warming the hand or moving to an earlobe or forehead, while treating what the patient shows you.

quiz.q: An 82-year-old's Korotkoff sounds begin at 186, disappear at 158, return at 122, and finally vanish at 78. What has occurred and what is the true pressure?
choices: Pulsus paradoxus, and the pressure is 122/78
Equipment failure, and the reading should be discarded
Venous congestion, and the pressure is 186/158
An auscultatory gap, and the true pressure is 186/78
quiz.why: A silent stretch between phases is the auscultatory gap, and the true systolic is the first sound at 186 with the diastolic at the final disappearance of 78. Reading 122/78 is the classic falsely low systolic that happens when you inflate inside the gap; pulsus paradoxus is an inspiratory drop, not a silent window.

quiz.q: A seated patient has an unsupported back, crossed legs, and is chatting while you measure. What is the rough combined effect?
choices: About 20 mmHg too low
About 20 mmHg or more too high
No net effect, since the errors cancel
Unpredictable and impossible to estimate
quiz.why: An unsupported back adds roughly 5 to 8 mmHg, crossed legs another 5 to 8, and talking 10 or more, all in the same upward direction. They stack rather than cancel, which is how a normotensive patient gets labelled hypertensive.

quiz.q: An 88-year-old reads 218/94 with no headache, no visual change and no chest pain, and the radial pulse is still palpable with the cuff inflated to 235. What should you consider?
choices: Pseudohypertension from heavily calcified arteries
An auscultatory gap producing a falsely high systolic
A cuff that is too large for the arm
Pulsus paradoxus
quiz.why: A radial pulse persisting above the recorded systolic suggests arteries too calcified for the cuff to compress, so the gauge reads far above the true intra-arterial pressure. An auscultatory gap produces a falsely low systolic, an oversized cuff reads low, and pulsus paradoxus is an inspiratory variation.

quiz.q: A 4-year-old with a forearm fracture lies very still, does not cry, and avoids eye contact. What is the most likely explanation?
choices: He is comfortable and the fracture is not painful
He is asleep
Children in severe pain often withdraw and go still rather than cry
Pain scales do not apply under age 5
quiz.why: A quiet child is systematically misread as a comfortable one, and withdrawal is a recognised severe-pain behavior in children. FACES is usable from about age 3 and FLACC covers observation, so a tool clearly applies here.

quiz.q: Which tool is designed to score pain by observation in an intubated, critically ill adult?
choices: FLACC
CPOT
Wong-Baker FACES
Numeric 0 to 10
quiz.why: CPOT scores facial expression, movement, muscle tension and ventilator compliance, which is why it fits an intubated adult. FLACC is built for young children and nonverbal patients, and both FACES and the numeric scale require self-report.

quiz.q: A patient with a known sickle cell crisis rates his pain 10 out of 10 while his vitals are entirely normal. What is the correct response?
choices: Document normal vitals and defer treatment
Reduce the score to match the vital signs
Treat the reported score, since vitals adapt and this population is documented as undertreated
Score him with PAINAD instead
quiz.why: Vital signs adapt within hours, so normal numbers never rule out severe pain, and patients with sickle cell disease have a well-documented history of being disbelieved and undertreated. Self-report is the reference standard, so an observational tool like PAINAD is neither needed nor appropriate here.

quiz.q: In which direction do you pull the ear before inserting a tympanic thermometer in a 2-year-old?
choices: Up and back, as in adults
Straight out
Straight forward
Down and back
quiz.why: In children under about 3 the canal is straightened by pulling down and back, while adults require up and back. Using the adult maneuver on a toddler misaims the probe and produces a falsely low reading.

quiz.q: A patient found in a snowbank has a thermometer that displays LO. What does this tell you?
choices: The temperature is below the device's range, so a low-reading thermometer and a core route are needed
The temperature is exactly 34.0 C
The battery has failed
The patient is normothermic
quiz.why: Many standard clinical thermometers floor near 34 C, so LO means only below my range and gives no usable value. Suspected hypothermia requires a low-reading device and a rectal or esophageal route before any number drives a decision.

quiz.q: A patient with a suspected serious infection took ibuprofen four hours ago and now has a temperature of 37.1 C. What should you do?
choices: Chart the antipyretic and its timing alongside the temperature
Record the temperature as fever regardless
Ignore the medication, since it wears off in an hour
Repeat the temperature by the axillary route for confirmation
quiz.why: Acetaminophen or ibuprofen taken hours earlier can mask a fever completely, so the drug and its timing must sit next to the value for it to be interpretable. Recording a fever that was not measured is falsification, and an axillary repeat only adds a less accurate route.

quiz.q: A hypothermic patient being rewarmed moves from 31.2 C to 33.0 C to 34.4 C while the heart rate goes 44 to 52 to 60. How is this read?
choices: Deterioration, because the heart rate is rising
An unrelated arrhythmia developing
A drug effect requiring reversal
Appropriate response to rewarming, with rate rising alongside temperature
quiz.why: A cold heart beats slowly, so a rate climbing in step with the core temperature is the expected physiologic response to rewarming. These patients are still handled gently throughout, because a cold myocardium is irritable, but the trend itself is reassuring.

quiz.q: Which pair of measures typically turns abnormal before either of their component numbers does?
choices: Temperature and respiratory rate
SpO2 and EtCO2
Pulse pressure and shock index
Heart rate and systolic blood pressure
quiz.why: Pulse pressure and shock index each combine two values, so they capture a change in the relationship between them before either one crosses its own threshold. Heart rate and systolic pressure are the components, which is exactly why they move later.

quiz.q: A postoperative patient on 2 L moves from RR 18 to 12 to 8 while SpO2 goes 98%, 96%, 93%. Why did the saturation move so little?
choices: The oximeter probe was faulty
Supplemental oxygen keeps the saturation propped up, so it moves late
Opioids do not affect oxygenation
A respiratory rate of 8 is adequate ventilation
quiz.why: Supplemental oxygen fills the reservoir and masks hypoventilation, so the saturation drifts down slowly while carbon dioxide climbs unseen. The respiratory rate is the number carrying the signal here, and a rate of 8 is frank hypoventilation.

quiz.q: A patient at 30 weeks gestation has an EtCO2 of 30 mmHg and is not in distress. How do you interpret that?
choices: Hyperventilation from anxiety requiring coaching
Evidence of pulmonary embolism
A normal pregnancy value, from the physiologic rise in tidal volume
Equipment error, since EtCO2 cannot be below 35
quiz.why: Tidal volume rises 30% to 40% in pregnancy, producing a mild chronic respiratory alkalosis with an arterial carbon dioxide near 30 mmHg. Treating a normal pregnancy value as hyperventilation or embolism sends you after a problem that is not there.

quiz.q: A patient at 34 weeks involved in a rollover crash has BP 116/72 and HR 106. Why is a normal blood pressure not reassuring?
choices: Blood pressure is never useful in trauma
She can lose 1,500 to 2,000 mL before her pressure falls, because uterine circulation is sacrificed first
Pregnancy raises blood pressure, so 116/72 is already low
The heart rate of 106 rules out bleeding
quiz.why: The extra 1 to 1.5 L of blood volume in pregnancy is a reserve shunted away from the uterus first, so fetal distress can precede any maternal vital sign change. Pregnancy lowers rather than raises blood pressure, and a rate of 106 is itself within the expected pregnancy elevation, not a reassurance.

quiz.q: A conditioned cyclist whose usual resting pulse is 42 now has a heart rate of 96 after a fall. How should that be read?
choices: A large relative tachycardia that may be the only early sign of a problem
Normal, since 96 is within 60 to 100
Evidence of an underlying arrhythmia requiring cardioversion
A benign training-related finding
quiz.why: Judged against his own baseline of 42, a rate of 96 has more than doubled, which is a substantial physiologic response hidden inside a normal-looking population range. Benign training findings are things like sinus bradycardia and first-degree block at rest, not a doubling after an injury.

quiz.q: Reviews of in-hospital deterioration consistently show which failure in the hours before an arrest?
choices: Vital signs were never measured
Monitors malfunctioned undetected
Staffing levels made measurement impossible
Abnormal vital signs were recorded but nobody escalated
quiz.why: The repeated finding is that abnormal numbers existed in the chart for 6 to 8 hours and were not communicated to someone who could act. That makes escalation, not measurement or equipment, the skill that changes outcomes.

quiz.q: A NEWS2 total is 4, but the respiratory rate alone scores 3. What response does the tool call for?
choices: Routine monitoring, since the total is under 5
Urgent review, because any single parameter scoring 3 triggers it
Emergency response with critical care, since a 3 equals a total of 7
Repeat the score in four hours
quiz.why: The system triggers urgent review on a total of 5 to 6 or on any single parameter scoring 3, precisely so one extreme derangement is not diluted by normal values elsewhere. A total of 7 or more is what escalates to an emergency response.

quiz.q: You have raised a concern about a systolic of 84 twice and the response has not addressed it. What is the expected behavior?
choices: Accept the answer and document that you reported it
Wait for the next scheduled vitals check
Escalate up the chain, because the two-challenge rule expects it
Repeat the same concern a third time to the same person
quiz.why: The two-challenge rule says that after two unaddressed concerns you go up the chain, and most policies treat that as expected behavior rather than insubordination. Waiting or repeating to the same person leaves the patient in the same position that reviews identify as the failure point.

quiz.q: Which entry best documents an escalation?
choices: 14:32 BP 84/52, HR 122, skin cool and pale. Notified RN Grant. 14:34 RN at bedside.
BP low, nurse told.
Patient appeared unwell this afternoon.
quiz.why: The full entry records what was found, the time, who was notified, and what happened next, which is the part of the story a bare vital sign leaves out. A timed vitals line alone documents the finding but not the communication, and vague notes document neither.
